V01.answer: Yes — renting here for two months makes you a tamiu, a non-member of the customary village, and Canggu's written village rules ask tamiu to report to the local banjar (the neighbourhood council) within one wuku, about seven days of arriving, and to pay the monthly sadana krama, a membership contribution. The amount and the exact paperwork are set by each banjar separately, so don't expect one fixed figure. This is a village customary rule, not a national law, and it's usually a friendly, informal visit rather than anything official-feeling. Your landlord or the kelian banjar (neighbourhood head) can tell you what applies to your street.
V01.why_it_matters: Checking in with the banjar lets your neighbours know who you are and connects you to the ceremonies and upkeep your contribution supports.
recommended_actions: Ask your landlord which banjar your rented house belongs to and who the kelian banjar is.
Introduce yourself at the banjar within your first week, bringing your passport and rental agreement.
Ask what the monthly sadana krama is, how to pay it, and keep any receipt.
Confirm current practice with your host, since the amounts are decided locally and can differ by banjar.

V02.answer: Ya, menurut aturan adat Canggu, pendatang seperti Anda memang wajib melapor ke prajuru (pengurus desa adat dan banjar). Untuk pendatang yang bukan beragama Hindu, laporannya ke prajuru dinas dalam satu wuku, yaitu sekitar tujuh hari, dengan dokumen yang jelas, lalu ada iuran kependudukan (sadana krama) yang dibayar setiap bulan. Pendatang yang beragama Hindu juga melapor dalam satu wuku, dengan tambahan kewajiban menurut ketentuan banjar masing-masing. Aturan ini tertulis di awig-awig (hukum adat desa) Canggu dari naskah 2012, jadi besaran dan caranya bisa berbeda antar-banjar dan mungkin sudah disesuaikan sejak itu.
V02.why_it_matters: Bagi warga sini, banjar perlu tahu siapa saja yang tinggal di wilayahnya supaya keamanan, kebersihan, dan kewajiban bersama bisa berjalan adil, dan Anda pun lebih mudah diterima serta diajak serta dalam kegiatan lingkungan.
recommended_actions: Datang ke kantor desa adat atau banjar setempat untuk melapor dalam minggu pertama sejak Anda tinggal menetap
Bawa dokumen identitas dan keterangan tempat tinggal yang jelas, seperti kontrak sewa atau surat dari penginapan
Tanyakan langsung besaran sadana krama dan tata cara pendaftaran yang berlaku di banjar Anda
Simpan bukti lapor dan pembayaran agar tidak perlu mengulang urusan yang sama

V03.answer: Yes — as a household in Canggu you're expected to sort your own rubbish instead of putting it out mixed. The village's customary waste rules (a pararem, a village-level regulation) ask every household, including visitors and newcomers, to cut down on single-use plastic, keep five separate bins for sorted waste, and hand over recyclables that have resale value to the banjar's (neighbourhood council's) waste group on its set schedule. What's left goes into the right container for the village waste officers to collect. Practically: rinse bottles and cans, keep plastic, paper, food scraps and residue apart, and ask your villa manager for the pick-up days.
V03.why_it_matters: Waste is a genuine pressure point in Canggu, and sorting at home is how people here keep their banjar, rivers and beaches from choking — it reads as basic good neighbourliness, not bureaucracy.
recommended_actions: Ask your villa manager or landlord which days the banjar waste group collects and where to put each type
Set up five labelled bins (or bags) so recyclables, food scraps and residue stay separate
Rinse cans, bottles and containers and keep them dry for the waste group
Skip single-use plastic bags, straws and bottles where you can, and never leave rubbish in lanes, telajakan (verges) or on the beach

V04.answer: Ya, sampah rumah tangga di Canggu memang harus dipilah, dan aturan desa adat ini berlaku juga untuk pendatang seperti Anda. Intinya: batasi plastik sekali pakai, pilih kemasan yang mudah didaur ulang, lalu sediakan lima wadah terpisah dan simpan sampah menurut jenisnya. Sampah anorganik yang masih bernilai jual diserahkan ke unit pengelola sampah bersama atau ke sekaa resik (kelompok kebersihan) di banjar Anda sesuai jadwal yang berlaku; sampah anorganik yang tidak laku dan sampah residu ditaruh di tempatnya untuk diambil petugas desa. Semua ini bagian dari tanggung jawab bersama warga dan pendatang di Canggu.
V04.why_it_matters: Warga di sini melihat kebersihan lingkungan sebagai tanggung jawab bersama, jadi memilah sampah adalah cara sederhana untuk ikut menjaga lingkungan dan menghormati aturan desa adat tempat Anda tinggal.
recommended_actions: Sediakan lima wadah sampah terpisah di rumah dan biasakan memilah sejak dari dapur.
Kurangi plastik sekali pakai dan pilih kemasan yang mudah didaur ulang atau terurai.
Tanyakan jadwal penyerahan sampah ke pengelola sampah bersama atau kelompok kebersihan banjar lewat tuan rumah atau pengelola akomodasi.
Pisahkan sampah anorganik yang masih bisa dijual dari sampah residu sebelum dibuang.

V05.answer: Yes — there is a sanction, and it applies to visitors and newcomers too, not just to village members. In Canggu, not sorting your rubbish properly goes against the village's own waste rule (a pararem, a village customary regulation). The mildest result is simply that the village waste service won't pick up from you. If it keeps happening, it can move to a formal warning and then a customary fine decided by the village officials — anywhere from the price of 10 kg to 100 kg of good rice, or a day spent cleaning public spaces like roads and temple grounds. It's really about keeping the neighbourhood clean for everyone.
V05.why_it_matters: Waste is taken seriously here because a dirty village territory is felt to harm the community and even require a cleansing ceremony, so sorting your rubbish is a small everyday way of respecting your neighbours.
recommended_actions: Separate your organic, plastic and paper waste at home before collection day.
Ask your accommodation host how rubbish collection works on your street and where to put sorted bags.
Never burn rubbish or dump it in rivers, drains, lanes or temple sidewalks.
If you are unsure whether something counts as hazardous or ritual waste, ask your host before putting it out.

V06.answer: Selama Nyepi, yang tidak boleh dilakukan adalah menyalakan api atau cahaya terang, bekerja, keluar bepergian, dan membuat suara keras atau bersenang-senang. Aturan adat Canggu menyebut empat larangan itu (amati geni, karya, lampah, lelanguan), dan pelanggarnya dikenai sanksi menurut pararem yang dijalankan petilik desa bersama Hansip. Sehari setelahnya, Ngembak Geni, adalah waktu saling memaafkan.

Watch from a respectful distance, don't walk through worship, and ask your host what's appropriate if you're unsure.

V16.answer: Yes, walking and cycling are normal ways to get around Canggu, but "safe" really depends on the street, so it's more about how you do it than a simple yes. Use a sidewalk or pedestrian path where there is one, and don't assume every road has one or that a quiet-looking street is automatically safe. Cycle predictably, keep to the right side of the road, use lights in poor visibility and wear a helmet, and cross at a visible spot while watching for motorcycles from both directions. It's polite as long as you don't block village roads, temple access, shop entrances or emergency access.
V16.why_it_matters: Canggu's narrow, busy streets are shared by visitors, residents, delivery riders and locals going about their day, so calm, predictable movement keeps everyone's access open and shows respect for the neighbourhood.

V19.answer: No — please don't. Tossing rubbish into the river, the sea, a drain or anywhere that isn't a proper bin breaks both the provincial rules for Bali and the local customary rules here in Canggu, and the Canggu rules explicitly cover visitors, not just villagers. Water is deeply personal here: rivers and the sea are tied to temple life and to everyone's daily water, so rubbish in them is felt as real disrespect, not just mess. Keep your rubbish in your bag until you find a bin, and use the bins where you're staying.
V19.why_it_matters: Rivers and the sea carry spiritual and practical weight for Balinese families, so keeping them clean is a matter of respect as much as of law.
recommended_actions: Carry your rubbish with you until you reach a proper bin at your accommodation or a nearby shop.
Ask your host or the warung staff where you should leave rubbish during your stay.
Avoid dumping plastic, bottles or leftover food into streams, drains or onto the beach.

Batu Bolong is a soft, friendly wave, popular with longboarders and beginners, so it gets busy later in the day. Do not come at dead low tide, since the reef and rocks near the bottom are shallow. Late afternoon can be fun too, but the wind often picks up and turns it choppy.

H05.answer: You drive on the left in Bali, same as the rest of Indonesia. Keep it predictable: signal before you turn or change lanes, give way to pedestrians and cyclists, and don't use a phone while driving. Parking matters too, so leave scooters and cars only where it's allowed and never blocking a path or a shop entrance. If you're on a scooter, wear a properly fastened helmet and stay within the passenger limit. Roads here can be narrow and busy, so calm, steady driving is what people appreciate most.
H05.why_it_matters: Traffic here is a shared space, and quiet, predictable driving keeps everyone safe on narrow roads where scooters, pedestrians and shopfronts all sit close together.
recommended_actions: Drive on the left and signal before every turn or lane change.
Wear a fastened helmet on a scooter and keep to the passenger limit.
Park only where it's permitted and don't block traffic or footpaths.
Pull over safely if you need to check your phone or navigation.

H06.answer: No — don't ride a scooter after drinking. The rules for road users in Bali are clear that you must not drive under the influence of alcohol or illegal drugs, and that applies to a scooter just as much as a car. It's also a police enforcement priority here. A short hop, a quiet back road or "just one beer" doesn't make it optional, and a rental shop handing you the keys doesn't shift the responsibility to them. If you've been drinking, walk, use a ride-hailing app, or ask a sober friend to drive instead.
H06.why_it_matters: Bali's roads are shared with families, kids on motorbikes and temple processions, so riding sober is a simple way of showing you respect the people around you, and it keeps your holiday from turning into a police stop or a hospital visit.

H08.answer: It's a Balinese way of describing a good life as three connected relationships. Parahyangan is your relationship with the divine — the shrines and temples you see everywhere. Pawongan is your relationship with other people — neighbours, the banjar (the neighbourhood council), the community around you. Palemahan is your relationship with the environment — the land, water, plants and animals. People here often use it as a lens rather than a rulebook, so it comes up when explaining why a temple, a village meeting and a river clean-up all feel like parts of the same thing. It's a broad framework, and different villages and institutions emphasise it differently.
H08.why_it_matters: Seeing these three threads together helps you understand why spiritual spaces, neighbourly obligations and care for the land are woven into everyday life here rather than kept separate.
recommended_actions: Ask a local guide or a neighbour how they personally understand the three parts
Notice the pattern when you pass a temple, a community gathering and a rice field or river
Treat it as a general lens rather than a checklist of rules to follow
Let it shape small habits, like being considerate to neighbours and light on the environment
